title: The Mission and Mercy
overview: Luke 10 presents a rich narrative of Jesus commissioning seventy disciples to spread the gospel, emphasizing the urgency of the harvest and the challenges of ministry. The chapter highlights the authority given to believers over spiritual forces and the joy found in salvation. It also contains the profound parable of the Good Samaritan, teaching the true meaning of neighborly love beyond ethnic and religious boundaries. Finally, the chapter closes with the story of Mary and Martha, contrasting active service with contemplative devotion to Christ’s word. Together, these passages reveal the heart of Christian mission, the nature of discipleship, and the call to love and serve others in the power of God.
structure:
**Verses 1-16: The Sending of the Seventy.** Jesus appoints seventy disciples and sends them out in pairs to prepare the way for His coming, instructing them on how to conduct themselves and respond to acceptance or rejection. This section underscores the spiritual authority and responsibility given to the disciples.

**Verses 17-24: The Return and Jesus’ Praise.** The seventy return with joy, reporting their success over demonic powers. Jesus affirms their authority but redirects their joy toward the assurance of their salvation and reveals divine truths hidden from the worldly wise.

**Verses 25-37: The Lawyer’s Question and the Parable of the Good Samaritan.** A lawyer tests Jesus on inheriting eternal life, leading to the parable that redefines neighborly love as active mercy, transcending social and ethnic barriers.

**Verses 38-42: Martha and Mary.** The chapter concludes with a personal encounter illustrating the balance between service and worship, highlighting the priority of attentive listening to Jesus’ teaching.

keyVerses.text: Therefore said he unto them, The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest.
keyVerses.significance: This verse emphasizes the vast need for gospel workers and the necessity of prayer for God to raise up laborers, highlighting the mission urgency central to the chapter.

keyVerses.text: He that heareth you heareth me; and he that despiseth you despiseth me; and he that despiseth me despiseth him that sent me.
keyVerses.significance: This verse affirms the divine authority given to the disciples, linking their message directly to Jesus and, consequently, to God the Father, underscoring the seriousness of accepting or rejecting the gospel.

keyVerses.text: And he answering said, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself.
keyVerses.significance: This summarizes the greatest commandments, framing the entire chapter’s teaching on love for God and neighbor as foundational to eternal life and Christian conduct.

keyVerses.text: And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
keyVerses.significance: The conclusion of the Good Samaritan parable, this verse calls for active mercy and compassion, defining true neighborliness as practical love beyond social boundaries.

keyVerses.text: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
keyVerses.significance: Jesus highlights the priority of spiritual attentiveness and devotion over busy service, teaching the enduring value of hearing and obeying God’s word.

characters.name: Jesus Christ
characters.description: The central figure who commissions the seventy disciples, teaches profound lessons on mission, mercy, and discipleship, and reveals divine truths about salvation and authority.

characters.name: The Seventy Disciples
characters.description: Appointed by Jesus to preach and heal, they represent the expanding mission of the gospel and demonstrate the power and authority believers have through Christ.

characters.name: The Lawyer
characters.description: A Jewish expert in the law who tests Jesus with a question about eternal life, prompting the parable of the Good Samaritan and a deeper understanding of neighborly love.

characters.name: The Good Samaritan
characters.description: A compassionate outsider who exemplifies mercy and neighborly love by caring for a wounded man, challenging social prejudices and redefining true neighborliness.

characters.name: Martha and Mary
characters.description: Two sisters representing contrasting responses to Jesus: Martha’s active service and Mary’s contemplative listening, illustrating the balance needed in discipleship.

themes.description: The chapter opens with Jesus sending out the seventy to proclaim the kingdom, emphasizing the urgency of gospel proclamation and reliance on God’s provision.
The disciples are given authority over demonic forces, illustrating the victory of Christ’s kingdom and the believer’s empowerment in spiritual warfare.
Through the Good Samaritan parable, the chapter teaches that true love transcends ethnic and religious boundaries, calling believers to active compassion.
The contrast between Martha and Mary highlights the need to balance service with devotion, prioritizing attentive listening to Christ’s word.
Jesus praises God for revealing divine truths to the 'babes' rather than the 'wise and prudent,' emphasizing God’s sovereign choice in salvation.

historicalContext: Luke 10 is set in first-century Palestine during Jesus’ earthly ministry under Roman occupation. The region was culturally diverse, with tensions between Jews and Samaritans, which the parable of the Good Samaritan directly addresses. Travel was often dangerous, as illustrated by the man attacked by thieves on the Jericho road. The sending of the seventy reflects Jewish rabbinical practices of sending disciples to teach, but Jesus’ instructions and authority surpass traditional norms. Hospitality customs were important, as seen in the instructions about accepting food and lodging. Politically, the Jewish people awaited a Messiah to deliver them, and Jesus’ mission challenged existing religious and social structures.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Emphasizes God’s sovereign election in sending laborers into the harvest and the necessity of faith and repentance. The parable of the Good Samaritan is seen as a call to grace-filled mercy reflecting God’s covenant love.

Highlights the distinct mission of the seventy as a precursor to the church’s global evangelism. The authority over spiritual forces is interpreted as a present reality for believers empowered by the Holy Spirit.

Early commentators like Augustine saw the Good Samaritan as Christ himself, who binds our wounds and provides salvation. The sending of the seventy symbolizes the spreading of the gospel to the Gentiles.

crossReferences.connection: Jesus’ teaching on the plentiful harvest and few laborers parallels Luke 10:2, emphasizing the need for prayer and evangelism.
The command to love one another as a mark of discipleship connects with the love of neighbor taught in the Good Samaritan parable.
The spiritual authority over demonic powers in Luke 10:19 aligns with Paul’s teaching on spiritual warfare.
True religion involves caring for the needy, echoing the mercy shown by the Good Samaritan.
The importance of hearing and responding to God’s word, as Mary did, is foundational to discipleship.

application: Pray earnestly for more workers to be sent into the spiritual harvest fields.
Trust in the authority and protection God gives believers when sharing the gospel.
Show active mercy to those in need, regardless of social or cultural differences.
Balance service to others with devoted time listening to and obeying God’s word.
Rejoice in the assurance that your name is written in heaven, not merely in spiritual victories.
Recognize that true discipleship involves both loving God wholeheartedly and loving your neighbor practically.
conclusion: Luke 10 challenges believers to embrace the mission of Christ with urgency, empowered by divine authority and guided by love. It teaches that true discipleship involves both active service and attentive devotion, grounded in the love of God and neighbor. The chapter’s enduring message calls Christians to pray for laborers, exercise spiritual authority responsibly, and embody mercy that transcends barriers. Ultimately, it assures believers of their secure place in God’s kingdom and invites them to live out the gospel in tangible, compassionate ways.

outline.heading: The Sending of the Seventy
outline.description: Jesus appoints seventy disciples and sends them out with specific instructions for their mission, emphasizing the harvest’s urgency and the spiritual authority given to them.

outline.heading: The Return and Jesus’ Praise
outline.description: The seventy rejoice over their spiritual victories, and Jesus redirects their joy to the assurance of salvation and reveals divine mysteries to the humble.

outline.heading: The Lawyer’s Question and the Good Samaritan
outline.description: A lawyer’s inquiry about eternal life leads to the parable that redefines neighborly love as active mercy, challenging social prejudices.

outline.heading: Martha and Mary
outline.description: The contrasting responses of Martha and Mary illustrate the balance between serving others and prioritizing devotion to Christ’s teaching.
